turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. Smith. It’s nice to meet you too. Um, well, to be honest, it’s been a really frustrating time lately, and it took me a while to actually make this appointment. What brings me in is that I just... I feel like I absolutely cannot settle in my own body anymore. It’s this constant, uncomfortable feeling, almost like my skin is too tight or I have this motor running inside me that I just can't switch off. 

I really notice it the most when I’m supposed to just sit quietly and do normal, everyday things. Like, since I'm managing the house full-time right now, I have to handle a lot of the paperwork and sit down to go over shared household plans. We try to set aside time to just sit at the kitchen table and go over the bills or the weekly schedule, which I should be able to do—I have a degree, I know how to read a spreadsheet—but I just... I can't stay in the chair. The paperwork will be right there in front of me, and I know I need to look at it, but my legs start bouncing, and I feel this intense, almost painful urge to just stand up or walk around. I’ll find myself making excuses to get up, like checking if the back door is locked or getting my third glass of water, because sitting still to handle those plans is just physically unbearable. It's exhausting feeling this keyed up all the time when I just want to sit and get basic things done, you know?

symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes feeling like they 'cannot settle in my own body anymore' and feeling 'keyed up all the time'.
symptom_reasoning.S013: The patient notes difficulty when they are 'supposed to just sit quietly and do normal, everyday things'.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes having a 'motor running inside me that I just can't switch off'.

turns.doctor_question: When you are trying to focus on these tasks, do you find that your mind frequently wanders or that you have trouble keeping your attention on the task itself, independent of the physical need to move?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, absolutely. Yes. It's not just the physical part, though that's awful. Even if I somehow manage to glue myself to the chair and ignore the urge to get up, my brain just... it just goes on vacation. It's incredibly frustrating because, like I said, I have a degree. I know I am capable of reading comprehension! 

But these days, I can sit down with, say, a long planning email from the school or my husband, or even just a chapter of a book that I actually *want* to read—like a novel I picked up because I thought, you know, I should try to relax more, let's read a mystery—and I’ll start out completely fine. For the first minute or two, I'm reading the words, I'm following along, and then... I don't even know when the shift happens, but suddenly I realize I've been staring at the exact same paragraph for I don't know how long. My eyes are physically moving over the text, but absolutely none of it went in. 

I’ll suddenly realize I’ve spent the last three pages thinking about what I need to defrost for dinner, or remembering a weird conversation I had with a neighbor last week, or wondering if I ever actually called the plumber back about the guest bathroom sink. And then I have to go back and re-read the email or the chapter from the beginning, and half the time it happens *again*. It’s like my brain just refuses to hold onto the information in front of me, no matter how hard I try to force it to just pay attention to the words on the screen.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly confirms difficulty sustaining attention, noting that when trying to read an email or a book, their brain 'goes on vacation' and they fail to absorb the information.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by unrelated thoughts, such as dinner plans or past conversations, while attempting to focus on a task.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient mentions struggling with an 'awful' physical 'urge to get up' and having to force themselves to stay seated, indicating internal restlessness.

turns.doctor_question: Have you experienced these difficulties with sitting still and staying focused in other areas of your life, such as at work or in social situations, or does this primarily happen when you are trying to manage household tasks?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it’s... it’s definitely not just the household stuff, unfortunately. I mean, that’s where it’s most obvious right now because that’s my main focus, but it bleeds into everything else, too. And it’s honestly causing a lot of problems, which is part of why I finally made this appointment. 

For example, I do a lot of volunteer work—or, well, I used to do a lot more. I’ve been involved with the PTA and this local community garden project for a few years now. And I really care about these things, I do. But lately, the fallout has been that the people there... they just can’t reliably count on me anymore. We’ll have these committee meetings, right? And I’ll be sitting there, trying so hard to pay attention to the agenda, but my leg is shaking, I’m shifting in my seat, and my mind is a million miles away thinking about the grocery list or whether I left the oven on. And because I’m so distracted and antsy, I end up missing important details or volunteering for things and then completely forgetting to follow through. 

I’ll say, "Oh, sure, I’ll organize the bake sale spreadsheet," and then three weeks later, someone asks me for it, and I haven't even started because I couldn't sit still long enough to get it done, or I just lost track of the email entirely. It’s so embarrassing. I feel like I’m constantly apologizing. I’ve actually had to step back from some of my roles, like I stepped down as the fundraising chair, because I just keep letting things fall through the cracks. And my husband, too—he gets so frustrated because I’ll promise to handle calling the insurance company or booking the summer camp, and then... I just don't. Or I start, get up to get a glass of water because I can't stand sitting on hold, and then I start folding laundry and forget I was even on the phone. It’s like, no matter how hard I try to just be reliable and get these things done, I can't, and it’s really affecting how people see me and how much they can trust me to handle things.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your childhood or your time in school, did you experience these same difficulties with sitting still and staying focused on tasks back then?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, wow. Um, looking back... yeah. Yes, definitely. It’s funny, because you think of this as an adult problem, or at least I did, because the stakes are so much higher now with the mortgage and the kids and everything. But if I really sit and think about it... this was already part of me way back in elementary school. 

I mean, I can picture my desk in third grade so clearly. Mrs. Gable's class. It was an absolute disaster zone. Every other kid had these neat little stacks of folders and their pencils in the little groove at the top, and mine was just... an explosion of crumpled papers, broken crayons, half-finished drawings. I could never find anything. And the permission slips! Oh my gosh, my poor mother. I was always the girl who forgot to bring the slip home, or I’d bring it home, she’d sign it, and then it would just vanish into the black hole of my backpack and I’d be the only kid who couldn't go on the field trip to the zoo until the office called her at work to give verbal consent. 

And the sitting still... yeah. I was constantly getting in trouble for that. I remember so many report cards coming home with those little checkmarks next to "Needs Improvement" for self-control or whatever they called it back then. My teachers were always writing notes saying I talked out of turn, or I was interrupting other students, or I just seemed completely unable to stay seated during quiet reading time. I’d always be up sharpening my pencil—even if it was already sharp—or going to the bathroom, or just kind of hovering by the bookshelf because sitting in that little plastic chair felt like torture. It’s actually really wild to think about it now, because it’s the exact same feeling I get when I’m trying to sit at the kitchen table with the bills. Just this... this absolute inability to just stay put and do the thing I'm supposed to be doing. So, yeah, it’s definitely not new, even if it feels more overwhelming now.
